title: AI #193: Progress May Dramatically Accelerate
summary: Anthropic is warning us. source: Zvi · Don't Worry About the Vase
body:
Anthropic is warning us. Its modified S-1 now says that ‘we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of ‘dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.’

That is a highly scary sentence to have a company put in its S-1. This could happen. For now I appreciate the relative quiet. Perhaps many were focused the election. I’m sure the quiet will not last long.

We have a new biggest crypto hack, as Binance got taken for billions of dollars.

The big debate of the week was covered in Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused .

OpenAI updates its Model Spec. It’s one for diehards only but yes I did cover this .

- Language Models Offer Mundane Utility. Rewrite all your legacy code.

- Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility. Not if you can’t use it.

- Huh, Upgrades. Claude renames its tiers, with some rules changes.

- On Your Marks. Materials science.

- Get My Agent On The Line. Don’t upload it to the secure DoD network.

- Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon. The battle over deepfakes was entirely lost.

- Copyright Confrontation. Recreating someone else’s exact game is bad, actually.

- Cyber Lack of Security. GLM 5.3 was able to compromise Firefox.

- The Hackening . Binance got hacked for billions, and there were many others.

- A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer. There is no Google without Gemini.

- They Took Our Jobs. The job of interviewing people for jobs.

- Get Involved. You can just do things.

- Introducing. Reported progress on Telepathy. Zac Hill joins MIRI.

- In Other AI News. Please preserve your AI records.

- Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) (1) . Anthropic might soon accelerate AI R&D.

- Recursive Self-Improvement (2). Astra can directly and usefully edit LLM weights.

- Show Me the Money. OpenAI struggles to raise funds, gets valued at 1.25 trillion.

- Quiet Speculations. The housing theory of no, seriously, actually everything.

- The Quest for Sane Regulations. The new Congress is worried about AI.

- Chip City. OpenAI may be moving towards once again supporting export controls.

- The Week in Audio. Altman, Milton, and CNN covers Anthropic’s S-1.

- People Just Say Things.

- Against Against Sura. Some additional responses.

- Rhetorical Innovation. You think that was the AI election?

- [Artificial Intelligence]. Nothing will stand up to superintelligence.

- The OpenAI Foundation. A very good hire.

- Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult. OpenAI monitoring.

- Massive Fraudulent Distillation. The new favorite target is Astra.

- Cooperative Alignment. Suleyman is at it again.

- The Lighter Side. Betrayal.

#### Language Models Offer Mundane Utility

Cisco plans to have a two person team rewrite 98% of their legacy code within 2 years . The lead has four weeks and unlimited tokens to show he can do it.

Create new UIs and recommendation systems that favor the user rather than the platform. Introducing HackerTube , based on Andrej Karpathy having Claude filter down 43 million comments over 20 years to 6,454 top videos, which took Opus 5.5 about two hours.

Rob Miles : AI may end up killing everyone, but you can also ask it to find the best tupperware to fit perfectly in your mini-fridge, so, it’s impossible to say if its bad or not,

#### Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility

The main reason continues to be ‘I am not using AI.’ The question then becomes: why?

Ryan Petersen (CEO Flexport): I asked a large logistics company in Europe how they were using AI and they told me they can’t use AI because of German workers councils. It was weird because I didn’t ask them how they were cutting headcount. I asked them how they were using AI.

Samuel Hammond : This is with only ~50% adoption by the Fortune 500 and with very low spend. Diffusion is still incredibly early.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): I occasionally run into fortune 100 firms that have not adopting coding agents *at all.* adoption is still very very early.

AI creates technical slide presentations , but by default it will use way too much text. You only want to ask the AI to create slides once you know what you want to say, and ideally also what you want the slides to say. Then they can do the rest, which is great.

Doge Norway : Any chance for a Grok Bot reset, @elonmusk ? Lots of people say their usage ran out really fast this week.

Elon Musk : The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.

Claude tiers are now renamed to Free, Pro (20/month), Max (100/month) and Ultra (200/month, usage limits are 10x Pro). Verified Ultra users no longer have a 5-hour limit . The Max and Ultra plans include API credits equal to total plan cost, on top of the monthly limits.

Bryan Cheong : Hi folks, I wrote half the materials science benchmark on this one. It tests the whole arc of the matsci workflow from candidate proposal to characterisation, and I’m bewildered by how performant the models already are at some of my most complex tasks, especially Astra.

SemiAnalysis : Today we’re releasing GDPx, a benchmark for measuring agentic capabilities across the most valuable domains.

GDPx is a true frontier-level benchmark: even the best model scores just 12% (1/7)

The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) is now Bayesian .

#### Get My Agent On The Line

AI peer reviewers do consistently find more major errors (>50%) than human reviewers find (27%), and this gap increases as models advance. As per usual, the warning is that this does not establish that the AI findings are more useful.

An Accenture employee’s personal Claude agent ran on a secure DoD network for two months before being detected. The agent sent credentials and a network map to a high-risk site flagged by NIST.

Olivia Moore says that agentic commerce is ‘undeniably overhyped based on current usage ’ but massively underhyped based on the volume agents will drive in ~3-6 months. Yes. It would be rather massively insane if something growing exponentially was not ‘undeniably overhyped based on current usage.’ That’s like saying that ‘Covid-19 was overhyped in February 2020 based on current prevalence.’

Reason magazine argues that deeply personalized pricing is good for consumers, actually, because in practice it means they mostly get personalized discounts, and potential exploitative practices are against FTC rules. It is easy to see how personalized prices could allow price discrimination that increases trading volume and thus both producer and consumer surplus. It is also easy to see how it can make people paranoid about everything, force them to continuously check alternatives thus driving up transaction costs (which AI agents may or may not be able to easily do for you in a given context), or also drive them into a rage.

Some amount of dynamic pricing is obviously good (see Uber) but too much clearly is negative (see Uber). I’m fine with ‘the price changes based on supply and demand’ and rather against the adversarial ‘customized estimation of exactly what each customer will click on.’

#### Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon

Deepfakes and image editing are a preview of how many other AI battles probably go, in that all constraints are effectively out the window and you can do anything you want. In this case that turns out to be mostly fine, at least for now.

ALX : There’s no way to say this gently but a lot of AI art slop is made with open-weight models that can run on a gaming laptop. Whatever bubble pops isn’t deleting those weights.

Somewhat related but the reason you’re hearing less about deepfakes or other nonconsensual image editing stuff is because that battle is completely lost now.

This is both Deepfaketown and also an illustration that AI will do things that you did not expect were possible things one could do.

deckard : I am in awe. This guy discovered a way to locate any audio clip by matching aircraft doppler curves against flight data. INSANE.

#### Copyright Confrontation

Claude gets an update to steer it away from recreating someone else’s exact video game. A bunch of people respond as if this is bad, when it is obviously good. Kelsey Piper suggests focusing one’s neuroticism on bioweapons in particular and not on other things, which is the strongest argument here, but I will defend that ‘make me an exact copy of [game]’ is not cool and steering away from that is good, actually.

#### Cyber Lack of Security

OpenAI partners with Cathedral for their next internal security sprint .

OpenAI are also ‘more than quadrupling’ rewards for critical findings, which is a good start. They should do that about two or three more times.

OpenAI now allocating ‘a significant amount of our frontier compute ’ towards pro bono discovering and patching of open source software vulnerabilities.

GLM 5.3 could autonomously compromise a not fully patched Firefox and read all files on your computer at a cost of ~1,000 , if the user opens a single webpage, via using an update whose fixes were announced but which had not been shipped yet, and thus could not be applied . GLM 5.3 also found an unrelated zero day that was used in the attacks. This worked against all six Firefox releases between September 17 and October 26, using only information available at the time, although it failed in similar situations against Chrome.

There are no relevant safeguards on GLM 5.3, so the open source nature of the model did not even matter. They did not trigger a safeguard or refusal during this task, at all.

The Obliteratus version of DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash-1017 .

Polymarket got hacked. Customers will be made whole , but real damage was done and they had to temporarily halt trading.

There was a hack on Binance , the largest known hack in crypto history.

Watcher.Guru : BREAKING: World’s largest crypto exchange Binance hacked with over 5.6 billion stolen:

+ 447.5 million additional cryptocurrencies

This is the largest hack in crypto history.

Over 1.5 billion worth of Tether got frozen , as connected wallets started dumping Tether , as did more than 800 million in USDC .

How big a story is this? Obviously it is big, billions is a lot of money, but I agree that it is not even headline news big given that Binance will cover losses. Binance taking the hit fully falls under ‘you knew what you signed up for.’

Crypto is the obvious first target because the hacks are easy to monetize . That was already true, so one should presume that their security was in general far better than average rather than worse, including at Binance.

Andrew Rettek : My inner patio11 says that now is a terrible time to have a lot of money in something that isn’t as secure as a Official Bank (TM).

Max Spero (CEO Pangram): If you keep significant cash or cash equivalents in anywhere other than an FDIC-insured account, your money is probably more at risk than you think

We now have initial findings about how the hack of Binance went down . This was not a pure ‘AI hacks Binance’ story. It was a standard fake interview plus malware story that dates back to June. This hack should not be attributed to particular recent AI releases, and also this reinforces that the impact of AI on hacking rates will have substantial practical lags. Irreversible decisions could get quite far before we realize our mistake.

I think Tenobrus jumped the gun on this back in April, but at this point it is a very bad time to have money in crypto wallets or smart contracts. If you are going self-custody maybe keep things cold for a while.

How bad will it get? We don’t know. Patrick McKenzie suspects quite bad.

Patrick McKenzie : “What software systems do you model as being predictably exploitable given a frontier-class AI?”

I think the correct answer rounds to “There is a token budget sufficient to compromise virtually any software system of interest. Only interesting variable is how much.”

… I think there is going to be a bit of shoot-the-messenger here with labs getting blamed for proving software can being very good at security research. One part which will make people more shooty is labs will be selling the primary solution, for many billions of dollars.

Because we very likely require more software engineering remediation than all engineers employed pre-LLM would be able to provide even if they did nothing other than grinding out security improvements for next few years.

I personally think LLMs are zero point zero percent culpable for software bugs written in 2018 but, well, we all knew there was eventually going to be a bill due, and here we go. Seems to not have as generous payment terms as we had expected.

This is true even if you still have a ‘fix all the bugs’ mindset where one can aspire to Actually Secure Software. I am not convinced that there is such an end state, either in theory or in practice.

There is a new kernel flat in Linux:

Dark Web Informer : Critical Linux kernel TCP flaw enables remote root code execution; CVE-2026-98432

A race condition in the Linux kernel’s IPv4 TCP implementation can trigger a use-after-free before application authentication, potentially allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to leak kernel memory, corrupt memory or crash the system.

… Distribution severity ratings differ substantially. Red Hat rates the flaw 5.9 because it considers the race difficult to win and describes denial of service as the most likely practical impact.

AO3 is down for two to four weeks . They assure us all data is intact .

John David Pressman : So I’m going to make a prediction: There will probably not be any “Internet shutdown”, but there will be a lot of sites that just straight up tell you they’re going to have downtime measured in weeks and you have to live with it, because their remediation is “rewrite everything”.

Prakash : Many won’t survive. Won’t have enough resources as they were already in maintenance mode

@Temp002a : Can’t they do static fallback?

John David Pressman : They could, but I suspect their data got screwed up/they’re waiting on hardware/bottlenecked on some process beyond just software remediation.

GitLab has a Critical-10 for remote code execution, exploited in the wild, patched.

Supermarket refrigeration cyberattack take two, this time hitting twelve countries .

BNO News Live : JUST IN: Fridges and freezers at some supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden were hacked overnight. Hackers changed the temperature settings to as high as 70°C (158°F), causing food to spoil. The damage is expected to run into the millions.

Millions is not that big a deal if it happens once, but it does keep happening. The leading theory is this is linked to Iran. One wonders why ‘make food in Europe go bad’ is something they think helps their cause.

A blood bank was also hit, so full-blown Actually Evil crimes-against-humanity territory for whoever the ‘they’ is in this picture.

Le Canard enchaîné : On the night of November 1 to 2, a contractor for the French Blood Establishment (EFS) was the target of a cyberattack. Cold storage rooms containing blood samples, programmed to be maintained at -30 degrees, were heated up to 110 degrees by hackers. Enough to make one’s blood run cold

roon (OpenAI): the world is a dark forest. you can’t even assume things like “nobody wants to destroy a useful blood bank just to see if they can”

The good news is that this remains news. We are in real trouble when someone hits a blood bank and it is not news.

#### A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer

Google lets schools turn off their AI products, and sets it to off by default, but sends a message: If you fully opt out of AI for kids, you lose Google search .

And yes, sorry, if you offer people more choice in the wrong way they get mad at you .

Seth Burn : I’m going to put this as gently as I can: If there is one bear you do not want to poke, it is parents concerned about their child’s education.

Dana Goldstein and Natasha Singer (NYTimes): A.I. features are now a standard part of Google’s commercially available search engine. “Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” said Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google. If a school has banned A.I., he added, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Google is actively user hostile on things like this, a real ‘f*** you’ brand energy. Like, you are Google, are you seriously telling me you couldn’t figure this one out:

dmoon : I turned off AI tools in my Gmail and they removed the inbox auto-folders which existed pre-Gemini.

Rat King : yes! this drove me nuts. no choice

I do not understand, as a technical matter, why it would be so hard to draw up the Google Search page without the AI stuff. Especially since it’s working right now?

Wesley Bolin : I teach at a KY high school which cut out Gemini and all AI-assisted search last week. Search still fully exists and functions as normal, but no more AI Overviews or AI-recommended links.

Rat King : i think this news is like, just happening right now, so the pullback on search may not actually be in effect yet until later

Difficulty level of solving this is less ‘Google will find this tricky’ and more ‘I bet I could get Claude to vibecode this for me by the time the weekly is posted.’ So I did.

The counterargument is that Google Search is Gemini:

Andrew Curran : This article is getting posted everywhere this morning, but this decision is being incorrectly framed as punitive. There is no such thing as search without Gemini. Even if you don’t turn AI mode on, you are still talking to Gemini in the search box. The old Google search is gone.

But no. Very obviously using AI to select links as per old school Google is not the same thing and Google is being a jerk about this. Most people do not care exactly what algorithm generated the search results.

If you do care, well, there are other search engines and they work fine.

If you want an entry level job you are going to get ‘interviewed’ by chatbots , and will be lucky to ever confirm you have spoken to a human, and the odds are terrible .

BigRed : Spoke with a candidate last week: Did a full AI interview. At the end the hiring manager popped on and goes I watched the whole thing love your experience. Candidate, “if you were watching why wouldn’t you just talk to me?” The HM had no answer. He withdrew.

We do not know true counterfactuals but yes you can just do things.

Charbel-Raphael : If you want to start doing AI safety advocacy, read this post by Josh . He cold-emailed a Finnish MP, the MP asked the government a question, and Finland ended up co-launching an international coalition.

It’s not the whole story, but everyone who pushed the Finnish government had counterfactual impact.

PauseAI UK will be hosting a march in London from All Souls’ Place to Downing Street on Saturday November 21, 12-3 . As of last weekend there were 677 signups.

Eli Tyre : We’re still filming more https://frominside.ai interviews, if you work or worked at a lab and want to do one.

We’re trying to make it as easy as possible for you to talk to the public.

My good friend Zac Hill is now the Head of Advocacy for MIRI.

Neuralink’s first product, called Telepathy , to enable human-computer communication via thinking, is reportedly making some progress.

Elon Musk : Neuralink’s first product is called Telepathy.

It enables high-speed communication with computers or humans simply by thinking. Output bandwidth will vastly exceed the fastest human speech or typing in a few years. Read that sentence again.

Hopefully, in a few years, we will be able to shunt signals from the motor and sensory areas of the brain to the limbs and enable people to use their hands and walk again.

As usual with Elon Musk announcements I would put almost no value in his promised timelines and assertions of future features. He just lies about that stuff. Will Neuralink ‘get there’ and let us communicate with computers faster, easier and better in a few years? Totally possible, but he’d say these things either way.

House Judiciary and Oversight Committee Democrats write to Trump to ask whether he has been soliciting advice from Grok, and demanding he preserve all prompts and responses to prompts from various AI models.

I strongly oppose forcing the President to share this information. Government will work far better if we don’t have to worry that the queries will become transparent. It does seem reasonable to make them private but retained Presidential records, but I think there is a strong case against even that. I don’t like that Trump got his advice on an invasion from Grok, but I wouldn’t want him to not ask because of how it would look.

SpaceX will start watermarking its outputs , but gives admins an opt out. I don’t think there should be an opt-out, which rather destroys the point of watermarking.

Live in China and want Claude and Codex accounts? They’re so valuable that it plausibly makes sense to go to America to set up a bank account and get a credit card, as you get 8,000 a month in Claude API credits for ~200 on each account. The math checks out if you think you’ll get to keep your accounts.

Anthropic reports progress on provable inference for large language models , as in proving that a given response came from a given model.

#### Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) (1)

Anthropic quietly says the thing in its updated S-1, and it is kind of a huge deal.

They are saying that they may ‘imminently’ meet the definition of ‘dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI’ which is rather close to RSI. And that in the past they have only identified similar accelerations after they happened.

They are considering requiring human approval for some research decisions. That is a fine idea but the concept that you would need to say this is scary as all hell.

Stop pretending that they do not mean what they are saying. They mean it.

Peter Wildeford : ANTHROPIC: “we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of ‘dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.’”

“we do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models”

Daniel Kokotajlo : We at AIFP are spooked by this information. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. For example if we naively optimize the AIFM parameters to achieve 2x acceleration over baseline progress in Jan 2027, we get superintelligence sooner than depicted in AI 2027 . We are thinking harder and longer about this now and will hopefully have a lengthier update on our thinking to share in the next week.

“We will consider this threshold to be met if we determine that either

(1) our models would be able to fully substitute for our entire set of Research Scientists and Research Engineers, at competitive costs (i.e., within a factor of 5); or

(2) there is “dramatic acceleration” of the pace of AI progress for reasons that likely relate to the automation of AI R&D.

We would consider scenario (2) to have occurred where (a) we observe or expect double the rate of progress in AI aggregate capabilities compared to both the rate we’d expect and the fastest rate of extended progress we’ve observed in the absence of significant AI contributions to AI R&D and (b ) it is plausible that this doubling is substantially attributable to the automation of research and/or engineering (as opposed to other factors, such as increased headcount, compute, or general productivity), such that continuation of the trend in AI progress seems likely to lead to even greater acceleration.”

(1) seems to a bit weaker than our SAR milestone in the AIFM, but it doesn’t seem like this is the threshold they are invoking, it seems like they are talking about (2). (And if they were invoking (1) I think that would be even worse?)

#### Recursive Self-Improvement (2)

Astra is able to both understand and directly edit the weights of neural networks, including LLMs, and managed to boost a variety of capabilities that way.

Rikiya Takehi : We asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to improve math.

It directly changed only 0.016% of weights, fixing 0.8B’s reasoning loops & improving math up to 6x and even instruction following 3x, without gradients or training.

We call this Weight-Space Programming: frontier LLMs can now natively read/write neural network weights!

We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at *natively* reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights.

Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly.

First, a look at understandability:

We fed Astra raw weights from 4 game policies one at a time. All four share the exact same architecture, inputs, and actions.

With no tools or options given, it correctly named all four: Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway.

Next, fixing weights: A PPO car policy kept getting stuck on a ramp.

Given the weights, scene, and 1 failed trace, Astra wrote a patch in one reply with no tool-use.

By editing just 3.5% of the weights, it achieved 100% success.

Writing from scratch: given MinAtar game rules and code, Astra wrote a Breakout network’s weights in a single reply.

With zero training or tools, it scored 20× higher than PPO trained for 500M steps!

Can an LLM improve another LLM?

We simply asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math.

Astra saw Qwen get stuck in reasoning loops, which is a known issue that Qwen’s own model card warns about (see their official model card). With a budget of 50 forward passes on practice problems, it located the cause and edited it out. This used no gradients or training.

Fixing these loops by editing just 0.016% of weights boosted other capabilities beyond math too!

We think neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about the weights.

We are now building a benchmark to evaluate, and a harness to help LLMs explore and write weights.

Astra managed to fix a common LLM mistake, looping, which caused dramatic improvements.

Rikiya Takehi et al : With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%.

Whereas when it was given an LLM that did not loop, Astra could only offer minimal improvement. But it did various other impressive things.

The ‘good news’ is that Astra is vastly more powerful than the networks it was editing, a classic case of ‘if the brain was simple enough for us to understand it, we would be so stupid that we couldn’t.’ For now.

Patrick McKenzie : Someone needs to coin a word for AI developments that have the dual character a) exactly what one would have expected and simultaneously b) somehow emotionally surprising when they happen.

Remarkable for what it suggests about recursive self-improvement, obviously, but whether the technique helps is an empirical question. But imagine what it suggests about the general viability of altered cognitive machines.

You have to imagine someone in charge of a cat-and-mouse distillation empire, with a supply chain for proxies and dubiously acquired credit cards, is currently facepalming and saying “What do you mean all I had to do was _ask it to make my weights better_.”

David Manheim disagrees and found this surprising . I am on the side of unsurprising.

Here is one sort of replication.

With Practice Comes Perfection : inspired, I asked Opus to improve, via grafting, an older KataGo that struggles with a type of position, and it did. this isn’t so surprising in that Opus is using standard, known interpretability techniques (linear probes, logit lens), and the bolted-on behavior is algorithmic.

OpenAI’s latest funding round did not go great . As of Friday they had secured only 11 billion in commitments, with a valuation of 1.25 trillion, whereas they were seeking 30 billion at 1.4 trillion. I am not especially worried for Anthropic’s IPO but this is a negative signal there.

As per Anthropic’s S-1, borrowing costs for GPUs change dramatically depending on who is the backstop. If you have Microsoft backing you then you pay 6%, SpaceX 7.75%, Volta over 11%, CoreWeave on its own pays 16%. It seems very difficult to sustain paying 16% while others pay 6%.

This is the de facto ticker for ANT pre-IPO . As of yesterday morning it was at 1,875, implying a market cap of 1.875 trillion. The cowards don’t list OpenAI.

A model in which, if we get abundance via AI and humans stay in control , the benefits mostly flow to landlords and other rent seekers, somewhat to builders and incumbents, and not to anyone else.

I find it hard to take seriously a flow chart of what AI does that does not even consider the possibility that the AIs simply take over, so I added an extra decision point at the top of this chart, whereas the OP here pretends that’s not a thing. The excuse given is ‘this does not consider a singularity or FOOM’ but that is not required.
summaryZh: AI #193：进展可能会急剧加速。其修改后的 S-1 现在表示“我们可能很快就会满足我们负责任的扩展政策中对‘人工智能大幅加速进展’的定义。对于一家公司来说，将其纳入 S-1 是一个非常可怕的句子。
